query: Casting is the predominant fabrication method for high-entropy alloys, but solidification-related porosity and microstructural nonuniformity can cause heterogeneous properties. Studies of other high-entropy-alloy compositions have reported high hardness and notable compressive performance, yet these findings do not establish how to improve CoCrFeNiTi; moreover, some investigated alloys were brittle at 25 °C and displayed only limited plastic deformation at 600 °C. For equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi with a simple crystal structure, favorable plasticity and machinability, but low hardness and load-bearing capability, what single intervention could improve hardness and mechanical performance while preserving those favorable characteristics and clarifying the relationship between microstructure and deformation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, a quantitative prediction relative to the unmodified alloy, the processing and testing boundaries within which it should apply, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled microstructural and mechanical experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: Alloying with a refractory metal element, such as Mo or V, can improve the hardness and mechanical performance of CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy while preserving its favorable plasticity and machinability.
generation.intervention: Alloying with a refractory metal element, such as Mo or V
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a secondary phase, such as a Laves phase, due to alloying
generation.mechanism: The addition of a refractory metal element, such as Mo or V, can lead to the formation of a secondary phase, which can act as a strengthening mechanism, improving the hardness and mechanical performance of the alloy. This is derived from materials-science principles, as the formation of a secondary phase can lead to an increase in strength and hardness.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in hardness and mechanical performance, while preserving favorable plasticity and machinability
generation.baseline: As-cast CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy without alloying
generation.boundary: Alloying with a refractory metal element, such as Mo or V, up to a certain concentration
generation.uncertainty: The exact concentration of the refractory metal element required to achieve the desired improvement in hardness and mechanical performance is uncertain

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy samples with and without alloying with a refractory metal element, such as Mo or V. Test the hardness and mechanical performance of the samples at room temperature.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloyed samples do not show an improvement in hardness and mechanical performance compared to the unalloyed samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

A series of five-element CoCrFeNi-Nbx (x = 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, and 9 wt%) high-entropy alloys were prepared using high-energy ball milling and discharge plasma sintering methods. Then, the effects of doping with Nb elements on the organization and properties of the CoCrFeNi HEAs were systematically investigated by tensile testing, hardness testing, and examining their micro-morphologies. The results show that with the addition of the Nb element, the lattice distortion of the alloy due to the large size of the Nb atoms causes the microstructure of CoCrFeNi HEAs to change from a single-phase FCC structure to a dual-phase structure of FCC and Laves. With the increase in the Nb content, the increase in the volume fraction of the hard and brittle Laves phase leads to the enhancement of the HEA’s tensile strength, yield strength, and hardness, and a decrease in plasticity. The Nb5 alloy showed the most excellent comprehensive performance, with a tensile strength, yield strength, and plasticity of 879.1 MPa, 491.8 MPa, and 39.8%, respectively, and all the properties were improved compared with those of the HEAs obtained by the arc melting method. Strength and ductility (and hence toughness) are key mechanical properties of structural materials, although these properties are often mutually exclusive. In crystalline metallic materials, strength and ductility depend on the presence of crystal defects and how they move under mechanical loading. Dislocations serve as the prime carrier of plasticity in metals and their motion to create plastic deformation is strongly influenced by interactions with other dislocations as well as defects such as solute atoms, stacking faults, grain boundaries (GBs) and reinforcement particles or precipitates. In general, strong interactions (obstacles) strengthen a material although this often limits its ability to plastically deform. Twinning, however, appears to be a deformation mechanism capable of defeating this ‘conflict' between strength and ductility. The presence of twins usually serves to impede dislocation motion and induce strengthening, but multiple twinning systems can also enhance ductility. A variety of technologies have been used to prepare HEAs, such as thermal spray (TS) [], laser cladding [], and mechanical alloying (MA) []. Directional solidification (DS) technology has been used to prepare aero-engine turbine blades [], and the mechanical properties of materials have been improved [,,]. At present, DS technology has been used to prepare HEAs, single crystal HEAs have been successfully prepared, and the performance of HEAs has been improved [,].
